headline: Democrats take Congress, Canada's budget lands, jobs data diverge
summary: U.S. midterms flipped Congress and Trump responded by naming Stephen Miller chief of staff. Canada tabled its second Carney budget while losing jobs in October, as the U.S. added 165,000. Ontario focus stayed on student aid cuts and Toronto's budget gap.

top.headline: Democrats flip Congress; final House and Senate counts still firming up
top.what: Networks project Democrats will hold at least 259 House seats and at least 54 Senate seats; the Alaska and Mississippi Senate races are unresolved, with lawyers now involved in a razor-thin Mississippi count.
top.why: Democratic control of both chambers means the administration will face subpoenas, investigations and legislative roadblocks starting in January, and trade and tariff policy could be contested in Congress.

top.headline: Trump says U.S. may have to 'destroy' rest of Iran as war shadows post-midterm politics
top.what: Oil fell for several days on hopes of less war escalation after the midterms, but Iran says tankers caught fire near Hormuz and Trump has not ruled out more strikes.
top.why: Oil near or above US$100 is the main driver of higher inflation in Canada and the U.S., and it pushed the Bank of Canada to raise rates last week.

top.headline: Canada-U.S. trade talks continue as Democrats vow to repeal tariffs
top.what: Tariffs on Canadian goods remain while talks continue, and the DNC chair says Democrats would move to end them if they win power.
top.why: Ontario sells most of its steel and auto output to the U.S., so both a deal and the midterm outcome matter for factory jobs.

top.headline: Carney government's second budget projects $62.3B deficit with $142B in new spending
top.what: Finance Minister Champagne tabled the budget Thursday: a $62.3-billion deficit for 2026-27 and about $142 billion in new spending over five years.
top.why: The budget sets Ottawa's response to tariffs, deficits and defence spending, and the immigration targets shape population growth.

top.headline: With a $1.12-billion budget shortfall looming, Ford rules out a 'new deal' 2.0 for Toronto
top.what: Premier Doug Ford told reporters Ontario will not sign a new funding agreement with Toronto, as the city faces a shortfall of about $1.12 billion in its 2027 budget.
top.why: Toronto relies heavily on property taxes and fees, so a lack of new provincial or federal money keeps pressure on city budgets.

top.headline: Ontario's deficit swells to $16.9 billion as tariffs delay balanced budget
top.what: Ontario's fall update projects a record $16.9-billion deficit this year and $36 billion over three years.
top.why: Bigger deficits mean more borrowing and interest costs, which can squeeze future health, school and transit spending.

top.headline: Thousands of Ontario students walk out over OSAP cuts: 'We can't afford rent'
top.what: Thousands of students walked out over OSAP changes and tuition, while a separate freeze on student aid at career colleges drags on with no restart date.
top.why: Student aid and tuition decide whether many families in the GTA can afford post-secondary education and how much debt graduates carry.
